From: Mike Ruiz
To: Carlos Mendes
Date: Mon, 6 Dec 2021 09:14
Subject: Denver surgeon complaint - what to say

Carlos,

Sorry to hit you with this on a Monday but I need some guidance before AAOS regional next week. Dr. Whitaker's name keeps coming up - not one of ours, he's never been a paid consultant, but apparently he's been pretty vocal in the Denver market about seeing early revisions in his Apex patients. He's not shy about it either, and I heard secondhand he might bring it up on a panel or at least in the hallway conversations with other surgeons who are there.

I don't want to get caught flat-footed if someone asks me point blank "what about what Whitaker's seeing." Nashville rep here, not Denver, but a couple of my surgeons know him from residency and word travels fast in this specialty.

Can you give me something I can actually say if this comes up? I don't want to just shrug or change the subject, that looks worse. But I also don't want to say something that contradicts whatever Quality or Regulatory is telling people.

Appreciate any quick guidance, trying to get ahead of this before I fly out.

Mike

---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Carlos Mendes
To: Mike Ruiz
Date: Mon, 6 Dec 2021 13:52
Subject: RE: Denver surgeon complaint - what to say

Mike,

Good instinct to flag this before the conference rather than after. Here's the line we're using with the sales team - please stick close to this and don't freelance:

"Individual surgeon experience can vary based on patient selection, technique, and case mix. We take all clinical feedback seriously and monitor real-world performance continuously through our post-market surveillance program." That's it. Don't get into a debate about his numbers, don't try to explain them away, and definitely don't dispute what he says he's clinically observing - that's a fast way to make things worse.

If he or anyone pushes for more - trend data, comparisons, anything that sounds like a public statement - redirect to Dr. Adeyemi's office. Tell them Medical Affairs handles clinical inquiries like that, not sales. Do not try to answer it yourself even if you think you know the answer.

Let me know how the conference goes.

Carlos

From: Dr. Leon Adeyemi <ladeyemi@veridianortho.com>
To: Dana Okonkwo <dokonkwo@veridianortho.com>, Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>, Marcus Lee <mlee@veridianortho.com>
Date: Thu, 20 May 2021 11:42:08 -0400
Subject: RE: Final review needed: Apex objection handling FAQ v3

Dana,

I have reviewed questions 4 through 7. The technical framing is largely acceptable, but I must insist on a clinical modification to Item 6.

Under no circumstances should our sales representatives offer broad reassurance to clinicians or patients regarding adverse local tissue reactions. Given the published ARMD literature—particularly the documented progression of pseudotumor formation and abductor tissue necrosis even in minimally symptomatic patients—the FAQ must explicitly direct reps to state that any patient expressing concern should consult their operating surgeon to evaluate individual clinical and radiographic risk factors. We cannot have commercial personnel minimizing biological variability or implying these inflammatory cascades are benign.

With that specific sentence incorporated into the guidance for Item 6, you have my sign-off.

Leon

Leon Adeyemi, MD
Chief Medical Officer
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

Dana, Devon:

Per procedure, I pulled the complaint population through May 10 and reconciled the event coding against the MDR log. There are 41 complaints logged since August 2018 that include elevated cobalt and/or chromium, suspected metal debris/ARMD, unexplained pain with elevated ions, or early revision with a metal-ion finding. The current working set is TW-2019-0410 through TW-2019-0451.

The cases are not evenly distributed geographically. The initial concentration is in Atlanta, principally patients from Dr. Feld’s practice; there are also several Nashville cases associated with Dr. Rao. We should be careful not to imply provider causation from that concentration. Complaint narratives contain incomplete cup-positioning information in a number of files.

On the rate analysis, the complaint rate per 1,000 implanted systems is increasing quarter over quarter from Q3 2018 through Q1 2019. I have asked Supply Chain for final lot-level distributed/implant estimates because the complaint files do not consistently contain the implant lot. I can provide the preliminary table today, with lot reconciliation to follow.

For root-cause context, Tom’s February 2019 re-analysis at 55-degree inclination appears relevant. His results showed materially higher wear under that orientation than the standard 45-degree protocol. Quality has not concluded root cause; this should be described as an evaluated design/use-condition factor alongside surgical technique, patient selection, and component factors.

Attached: Apex_MDR_Complaint_Trend_2018Q3-2019Q1.xlsx

Priya

text:
VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
MEETING MINUTES

Registry Signal Review Meeting
Date: September 14, 2021
Time: 9:00–10:00 AM
Location: The Hub — Reserve B
Prepared by: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs

Attendees: Dana Okonkwo; Greg Novak; Priya Raman; Dr. Leon Adeyemi; Carlos Mendes; Marcus Lee; Rachel Steinberg
By phone: Rob Castellano, CEO

Purpose
To review the current ApexHip registry signal and determine whether continued commercialization with additional risk mitigation remains appropriate.

Discussion

1. Registry data. Greg Novak presented the March 2021 NJR annual-report data. ApexHip’s reported five-year revision rate is 7.1%, compared with a 3.2% class average. The difference remains after available review of age and head-size strata, although the registry does not permit a complete adjustment for surgeon technique, patient selection, or cup position.

Greg also reviewed the most recent AJRR extracts. The AJRR population is less mature than the NJR cohort, but the direction is consistent: an upward trend in early revisions, including records identifying elevated metal ions, ARMD, unexplained pain, and loosening among reported indications. Greg noted limitations in indication coding and data completeness. He recommended monthly monitoring until the next formal registry refresh.

2. Clinical interpretation. Dr. Adeyemi stated that the signal is concerning and warrants active mitigation. He did not believe the currently available registry information alone establishes a design defect or supports an immediate conclusion that all ApexHip recipients face the same level of risk. He noted that cup inclination, patient activity, and other clinical variables may be relevant to metal-on-metal wear and revision risk. His recommendation was closer monitoring, clearer surgeon guidance on patient selection and surgical technique, and prompt review of new clinical information rather than immediate market withdrawal.

3. Regulatory and complaint considerations. Dana Okonkwo reviewed the need to continue evaluating reportability and trend information under 21 CFR 803. Priya Raman confirmed that complaints involving elevated cobalt/chromium levels, ARMD, pseudotumor findings, unexplained pain, and revisions are being entered and assessed in TrackWise per procedure. Dana emphasized that complaint trending, MDR decisions, and registry surveillance must remain aligned and contemporaneously documented.

4. Commercial and communications considerations. Carlos Mendes and Marcus Lee discussed the operational impact of a withdrawal versus revised labeling and field communication. Marcus noted the need for clear, controlled guidance for the sales organization if ApexHip remains available. Rachel Steinberg requested that external communications accurately describe the available data and not characterize the registry findings as conclusive.

Decision

The group agreed to continue selling ApexHip at this time, subject to the following risk-mitigation measures:

• Implement a labeling update emphasizing appropriate surgical technique, including cup inclination angle, patient selection, and clinical follow-up considerations.
• Prepare a Dear Doctor letter for distribution to implanting surgeons in October 2021.
• Increase post-market complaint and registry trend monitoring.

Rob Castellano joined by phone for the decision discussion and concurred with the above approach.

Action Items

1. Carlos Mendes: Coordinate proposed ApexHip labeling revisions with Regulatory, Clinical, and Marketing. Initial draft due September 24.
2. Devon Mitchell: Prepare Dear Doctor letter draft for Regulatory and Legal review. Initial draft due September 27.
3. Priya Raman: Establish enhanced complaint-trend monitoring and provide a monthly summary to Regulatory and PMS beginning October 2021.
4. Greg Novak: Continue monthly NJR/AJRR surveillance and escalate material changes promptly.
5. Dana Okonkwo: Confirm regulatory documentation and review requirements for the labeling update and surgeon communication.

Dana

Subject: Performance Improvement Plan (PIP) — Complaint Handling Specialist

Purpose

This memo documents the Performance Improvement Plan for Denise Ferro, effective August 2, 2021, developed jointly by Priya Raman and HR following performance concerns identified during preparation for the June 2021 FDA inspection of the Warsaw facility. This document is confidential and should be retained in the employee's personnel file per standard Workday HR record retention procedure.

Background

During inspection-readiness review conducted the week of June 14, 2021, Quality identified a backlog of 47 open complaints in TrackWise assigned to Ms. Ferro's queue, several of which exceeded internal timeliness targets for MDR reportability determination. Per procedure QP-0091, reportability decisions are expected within 5 business days of complaint receipt, and complaint files are expected to close within 30 days absent documented extension. Ms. Ferro's queue showed a median time-to-decision of 14 business days over the prior quarter, and multiple files remained open beyond 45 days without documented justification. This contributed to one of the three observations noted informally by the inspection team regarding complaint trending timeliness, and is a significant compliance concern given 21 CFR 803 obligations.

Performance Expectations — 60-Day Plan (August 2 – October 1, 2021)

1. Reduce open TrackWise queue from 47 to fewer than 15 complaints within the first 30 days, and to a steady-state working queue thereafter.
2. Meet the 5-business-day reportability determination target on 100% of new complaints assigned during the plan period.
3. Close 90% of complaint files within 30 days per procedure, with any exception documented and approved by Ms. Raman in advance.
4. No missed or late MDR submissions during the plan period.

Support and Check-Ins

Ms. Raman will conduct weekly one-on-one check-ins (Mondays, 30 minutes) to review queue status, discuss any files at risk of missing timeliness targets, and provide coaching. HR will participate in a check-in at the 30-day mark to assess progress. Additional TrackWise refresher training has been scheduled for the week of August 9.

Consequences

Failure to meet the metrics above by the end of the 60-day period, or any new instance of a late MDR determination during the plan period, may result in further disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment, consistent with Veridian's performance management policy.

Subject: Registry data post-recall - any change in ApexHip revision trend?

Dana, Priya,

Following up two days out from the recall announcement. Wanted to flag something before it gets asked at a higher level.

The V-2200–V-2299 recall is a coating adhesion issue traced to plasma-spray drift at Cork — mechanically it's unrelated to the revision-rate signal we've been tracking out of NJR (7.1% at 5 years vs. 3.2% class average) and the AJRR data. That signal is driven by edge-loading wear and elevated Co/Cr, not coating flaking at inspection. Different failure mode, different population — the recalled lots weren't even implanted long enough to be in the 5-year registry cohort.

That said, I'd bet money plaintiffs' counsel will try to blur the two, and honestly some surgeons will too once they hear "recall" and "ApexHip" in the same sentence. Dr. Whitaker in Denver already conflates every Apex complaint into one bucket.

I think it'd be smart to get ahead of this with a short internal FAQ that clearly separates the coating issue from the metal-ion/revision-rate issue, in plain language, in case the board or comms needs to respond to press or surgeon questions. I can draft a first pass on the registry side if Priya can cover the complaint-handling angle and Dana can sanity-check the regulatory framing.

Let me know if this makes sense to prioritize this week.

Greg

Subject: NJR 2021 annual report - ApexHip revision rate flag

Priya, Dana, Devon—

The NJR 2021 annual report is now published. I pulled the relevant hip tables this morning and wanted to flag a finding that warrants more than an ad hoc email discussion.

For ApexHip, the reported five-year cumulative revision rate is 7.1%. The comparable class average for metal-on-metal hips in the report is 3.2%. There are limitations in the registry comparison—case mix, reporting lag, and relatively smaller Apex cohorts than the legacy systems—but the magnitude and direction are not something I think we should dismiss as statistical noise.

This also appears directionally consistent with the complaint trend Priya has been tracking in TrackWise: elevated metal-ion results, pain/effusion presentations, and revisions where ARMD or adverse local tissue reaction is noted or suspected. The registry data does not establish a mechanism, and not every complaint is a confirmed device-related event, but the two data streams are corroborating each other at this point.

I recommend we convene a formal cross-functional signal review rather than continue to address this through separate PMS, complaint, and regulatory discussions. Suggested attendees would include Quality, RA, Clinical, Design, Product, and Sales leadership. We should agree in advance on the data cut, the clinical questions, and the potential actions for consideration, including labeling and surgeon communications.

I can circulate a short briefing package with the NJR extracts, complaint-rate trend, and available revision narratives by Friday.

Greg

Re: Recall Status Report – Z-1418-2022, ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200 through V-2299

To Whom It May Concern:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. submits this periodic status report regarding its voluntary Class II recall of specified ApexHip acetabular cup lots, FDA Recall Number Z-1418-2022. The recall was initiated on June 14, 2022, following reports of KinetiCoat coating flaking observed during incoming inspection and product preparation.

The affected product consists of ApexHip acetabular cups manufactured at Veridian’s Cork, Ireland facility between November 2021 and February 2022. The affected lots are V-2200 through V-2299.

As of July 22, 2022, Veridian’s distribution and reconciliation records reflect the following:

| Category | Units |
|---|---:|
| Total units distributed | 1,140 |
| Units reported implanted | 412 |
| Remaining units subject to retrieval | 728 |
| Remaining units retrieved to date | 728 |

All known non-implanted units within the affected lot range have been accounted for and retrieved from domestic consignee inventory. Veridian continues to conduct effectiveness checks with customers and distributors to confirm receipt of the recall notification and completion of inventory reconciliation.

Veridian’s investigation identified plasma-spray parameter drift following a chamber maintenance event as the root cause of the adhesion deficiency. The condition affected the application process for the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating and may result in inadequate coating adhesion.

Corrective action has been implemented at the Cork facility. Specifically, Veridian has established a corrective maintenance verification protocol requiring documented confirmation of plasma-spray operating parameters following chamber maintenance and before release of product for routine production. The protocol includes enhanced process verification, review of chamber settings, and Quality approval prior to resumption of manufacturing.

Veridian will continue to monitor recall effectiveness and customer responses. A follow-up status report will be provided within 30 days.

Please contact me if the Agency requires additional information.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.
dokonkwo@veridianortho.com

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
Quality & Complaint Handling
Q1 2022 Complaint Trending Summary

Prepared by: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Date: April 1, 2022
Distribution: Devon Mitchell; Greg Novak
Product: ApexHip Metal-on-Metal Total Hip System
Reporting Period: January 1–March 31, 2022
Subject: Q1 2022 metal-ion complaint trending summary

Per the complaint-trending procedure, Quality reviewed all ApexHip complaints closed or opened during Q1 2022 with reported elevated cobalt and/or chromium values, suspected ARMD, tissue reaction, or revision associated with metal debris. Duplicate reports concerning the same patient event were consolidated where identifiable.

A total of 19 metal-ion-related ApexHip complaints were recorded during Q1 2022, compared with 12 during Q1 2021. The increase is concentrated in territories where the product has historically had greater utilization and where follow-up laboratory values are being obtained more consistently.

| Region | Q1 2022 Complaints | Revision Outcome Reported |
|---|---:|---:|
| Southeast | 7 | 5 |
| Nashville | 4 | 3 |
| Denver | 3 | 2 |
| Other | 5 | 4 |
| Total | 19 | 14 |

Of the 19 complaints, 14 include confirmation that revision surgery occurred or had been scheduled based on the latest information provided by the treating facility or surgeon. The remaining five reports involve ongoing surveillance, imaging, repeat laboratory testing, or a recommendation for clinical follow-up. Complaint files remain subject to update as additional operative and explant information is received.

Serum cobalt values were available in 16 of the 19 complaint records. The average reported serum cobalt level among those complainants was 41 ppb. This is materially above the generally cited normal range of less than 1 ppb in individuals without a cobalt-containing implant. Chromium values were also elevated in a majority of records, although reporting units and collection timing were not uniform enough to calculate a comparable aggregate without further normalization.

The observed trend continues to track with the pattern Halvorsen’s engineering team identified in prior wear testing, including increased wear under non-standard cup positioning conditions. Quality is continuing to process each event per procedure, including MDR assessment where applicable, and will provide the underlying TrackWise extract to Regulatory and PMS for their respective review.

Internal Memorandum

Date: February 11, 2019
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
To: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: ApexHip wear re-test results at 55 degree inclination

Priya, Carlos —

Wanted to get this in front of you before I go any further with it, because I don't love what I'm seeing.

Back at DR-3 in 2016 we locked the wear-test protocol at 45 degrees inclination only, per ISO 14242, and that's what's been in the DHF ever since. I've been sitting on a hunch since last fall that we should be checking off-nominal cup positioning too, since that's closer to what actually happens in a lot of real hips depending on surgical technique. So I had Meridian Labs re-run the protocol at 55 degrees cup inclination on a fresh set of cup/head pairs, same lot family as production, same head material (Co/Cr on Co/Cr).

Results are in — Meridian report MTL-19-0142, dated 2/6/19. Raw numbers:

- 45° inclination (standard, matches our cleared data): ~2.1 mm3 per million cycles volumetric wear, consistent with what we submitted in the 510(k).
- 55° inclination: ~9.8–12.4 mm3 per million cycles, depending on the sample. That's 4 to 6x higher than standard angle.

This is not subtle. The wear scar pattern on the cup rim at 55° is exactly the edge-loading signature I flagged in my concept-phase notes back in 2015 when we were still finalizing head/cup clearance tolerances — I'd predicted this could happen at high inclination but we didn't build it into the formal test matrix because ISO 14242 doesn't require it and DR-3 decided standard angle was sufficient for clearance purposes. In hindsight I think that was the wrong call, or at least an incomplete one.

I know this is a MoM system, so wear debris isn't just a mechanical problem — it's a Co/Cr ion generation problem, and higher wear volume at higher inclination is going to mean higher ion release in patients who end up with cups sitting steep, whether that's from surgical variability or from cup design geometry not tolerating it well.

Priya — has TrackWise flagged anything that could line up with this? I'm thinking about the Atlanta cluster from last August, three patients out of Feld's practice. I don't have visibility into implant positioning on those cases but if any of them were high-inclination placements this could be more than coincidence.

I want to be careful here — this is one lab run, small sample, and I haven't done the statistics properly yet (need to look at variance across the sample set before I say anything definitive). But the magnitude is big enough that I think we need to start looking seriously at either a design change to cup geometry (bigger clearance angle tolerance, maybe a modified rim profile) or reconsidering head material/size combinations to reduce edge-loading sensitivity.

Can we get 20 minutes this week to talk through next steps? I'd rather we get ahead of this than have it come up some other way.

Tom

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
National Sales Meeting 2018
ApexHip Positioning Deck — Speaker Notes

Presenter: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Date: January 18, 2018
Session: Reconstructive Portfolio Breakout
Distribution: Field Sales and Marketing

Slide 1 — Why Apex, Why Now

Open with the patient, not the bearing. The ApexHip patient is generally an active adult who expects to remain active: working, traveling, cycling, golf, family life. We have an opportunity to offer a modern total hip platform designed around stability, range of motion, and durable materials.

Do not frame ClassicHip as a bad product. It remains an important, proven option and is appropriate for many patients. The positioning is choice: ClassicHip is our established metal-on-poly platform; ApexHip gives the surgeon another option for the active, appropriately selected patient who values a large-head construct and a contemporary fixation platform.

Suggested line: “Apex expands the conversation beyond simply getting back to walking. It is designed for the patient who wants confidence in movement.”

Slide 2 — Differentiating the Platform

The three pillars are:

1. Stability through large-head options. Apex offers head sizes from 36 to 50 mm, allowing surgeons to select a construct that supports stability and range of motion.

2. Wear performance. In our ISO 14242 bench testing at standard 45-degree cup inclination, Apex demonstrated lower early wear rates than legacy systems. Keep this statement tied to the test conditions and use the approved leave-behind if a surgeon asks for data.

3. Fixation. The acetabular cup uses KinetiCoat porous titanium coating, acquired with KBT, to support bone ingrowth and initial fixation.

Avoid getting drawn into a head-to-head “winner” discussion with every competitor. We do not need to name brands to make the point. Most competitive systems can offer a large head or porous coating; Apex brings those features together in a coherent system backed by Veridian’s reconstructive organization.

Slide 3 — KinetiCoat: Make It Concrete

Reps should be comfortable explaining the coating in plain language. KinetiCoat is not paint and should never be described that way. It is a porous titanium coating applied to the cup surface to create a structure intended to support bone ingrowth over time.

Suggested language: “The goal is biologic fixation. KinetiCoat gives the surgeon a porous surface designed to help the patient’s bone engage with the cup.”

Do not overstate this as faster healing, guaranteed fixation, or superior fixation in every patient. Use “designed to support” and “intended to promote” consistently.

Slide 4 — Handling the Longevity Question

This is important: do not promise a specific number of years. We have bench data and a strong engineering rationale, but clinical follow-up for Apex is still short. Do not tell a surgeon or patient that Apex will last 20 years, 25 years, or “a lifetime.”

If asked, say: “Apex was designed with durability in mind, and the available bench testing supports its wear-performance profile. As with any newer system, long-term clinical follow-up continues to accumulate.”

Do not substitute a ClassicHip survivorship number for an Apex claim. The products are different, and surgeons will notice.

Slide 5 — Close

The ask is simple: identify the right surgeon and the right patient profile, lead with stability, wear performance at the validated test condition, and KinetiCoat fixation advantages. Be confident, be specific, and stay within the approved language.

If a question goes beyond the materials in the field guide, do not improvise. Send it to Product Marketing or Clinical Affairs and we will get an answer back quickly.

1. Purpose

This memo summarizes ApexHip complaint trending for Q3 2019 (July–September) per Complaint Handling Procedure QSP-014, and provides a comparison against Q1 and Q2 2019 volumes.

2. Complaint Volume Summary

Total ApexHip complaints logged in TrackWise for Q3 2019: 9. Of these, 4 are classified as suspected metal-ion/wear-related (elevated cobalt/chromium, pain, or suspected ARMD presentation), consistent with the pattern first identified in the Atlanta cluster (TW-2018-0311, TW-2018-0312, TW-2018-0319). No new Atlanta complaints were received this quarter; those three cases remain open pending explant analysis per procedure.

New complaints of note this quarter:

- TW-2019-0402 — Nashville, Dr. A. Rao's practice. Patient presenting with groin pain at 22 months post-implant; elevated serum cobalt reported by treating physician. Investigation ongoing.
- TW-2019-0417 — Denver, reporting surgeon Dr. J. Whitaker. Patient with joint effusion and suspected pseudotumor on imaging; revision surgery scheduled. Explant tissue requested per procedure.

Combined with the three Atlanta cases, this brings open metal-ion-pattern complaints to five as of quarter end, up from three at the close of Q2 2019 and two at the close of Q1 2019. The rate remains a small fraction of total units implanted to date, but the quarter-over-quarter increase warrants continued close monitoring per QSP-014 Section 6.

3. Relationship to Ongoing Engineering Evaluation

Quality is aware of the wear-test re-analysis conducted by T. Halvorsen (memo to P. Raman and C. Mendes, February 2019) identifying increased wear at 55-degree cup inclination relative to the standard 45-degree test condition. While no root-cause determination has been made linking specific complaint cases to inclination angle, Quality considers this analysis a relevant input to trending review and will continue to track complaint data against any engineering conclusions as they develop.

4. Recommendation

Based on current volumes and severity, Quality does not recommend a design change or field action at this time. We recommend:

(a) continued monthly trending review of ApexHip complaints per standard cadence;
(b) a follow-up periodic re-review of the metal-ion-pattern cluster at the close of Q4 2019, incorporating any explant findings from TW-2019-0417 and TW-2019-0402; and
(c) continued coordination with Regulatory Affairs regarding MDR reportability determinations on a case-by-case basis per 21 CFR 803.

MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: Quarterly Registry Review — Q4 2021 Update
Date: January 10, 2022
Time: 10:00–11:00 AM ET
Location: Hub, Conference Room 2B / Teams hybrid
Minutes prepared by: Devon Mitchell

Attendees: Greg Novak (Post-Market Surveillance), Dana Okonkwo (Regulatory Affairs), Priya Raman (Quality & Complaint Handling), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (CMO)

1. Purpose
This meeting was a scheduled follow-up to the September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review, to check whether newer registry data changes the picture that led to the decision to continue selling ApexHip with the labeling update and October 2021 Dear Doctor letter.

2. AJRR Q4 2021 Data (Novak)
Novak presented late-2021 AJRR figures. Revision rates for ApexHip remain elevated relative to the broader class average, consistent in direction and magnitude with the March 2021 NJR finding of a 7.1% five-year revision rate versus a 3.2% class average. Novak noted the AJRR dataset has a shorter follow-up window than NJR but the trend line is not moving in a favorable direction quarter over quarter. He cautioned against over-reading a single quarter but said two consecutive registries now point the same way.

3. Discussion — Is the Current Response Sufficient?
Okonkwo asked whether the label update and surgeon letter constitute an adequate response given the AJRR confirmation, or whether the company should revisit a design change (referencing the ECO-2019-118 proposal that was deferred in 2019) or a temporary sales pause pending further analysis.

Raman noted that complaint volumes in TrackWise have not shown a corresponding spike since the Dear Doctor letter went out, but acknowledged this could reflect underreporting or a lag rather than resolution.

Adeyemi stated that from a clinical standpoint the registry signal is concerning but that causation relative to surgical technique (inclination angle) versus device design has not been definitively separated, and that a sales pause is a significant step that should not be taken on registry data alone without further wear-testing correlation.

There was general discussion of the anticipated litigation hold, expected to be entered February 1, 2022, following Whitfield & Barr's engagement in January. The group agreed this development increases the importance of being able to show the company is actively monitoring and reassessing, but did not treat it as changing the substantive risk analysis.

4. Decision
No decision was made to alter the current course of action. The label update and Dear Doctor letter remain the company's position for now. The group agreed to revisit at the next quarterly review or sooner if AJRR or NJR data worsens materially.

5. Action Items
- Novak to prepare updated registry trend charts (NJR/AJRR combined view) for inclusion in the next board pre-read.
- Raman to continue monthly complaint trending and flag any deviation.
- Next meeting to be scheduled for early April 2022.

Minutes distributed to attendees only.

ENGINEERING TEST SUMMARY REPORT

Date: 18 April 2019
Prepared by: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
Product: KneeFlex Total Knee System
Subject: Meridian Testing Labs KneeFlex Wear Report Summary

Purpose

This report summarizes the final results from Meridian Testing Labs’ simulator wear evaluation of the KneeFlex tibial insert. Testing was run to the ISO 14243 knee wear simulation protocol through five million cycles. This is the production-intent UHMWPE tibial insert paired with the standard KneeFlex cobalt-chromium femoral component.

Bottom line: wear performance is where we expected it to be. No station showed an outlier trend that would require a design or material investigation.

Test Configuration

Meridian tested six stations using 10 mm medium congruent KneeFlex tibial inserts. The inserts were gamma-sterilized, packaged production-equivalent parts from the 2018 pilot build. Femoral components were standard polished Co/Cr components. Testing used bovine serum lubricant at the concentration specified in the protocol, with periodic lubricant changes and soak controls for fluid uptake correction.

The loading and motion profile followed ISO 14243 conditions. Inspections and gravimetric measurements were completed at one million cycle intervals. Meridian also performed visual inspection of the articular surfaces at each pull point.

Results

Corrected wear volume at five million cycles is summarized below.

| Test Station | Tibial Insert Size | Wear Volume at 5M Cycles (mm³) | Average Wear Rate (mm³/MC) | Observations |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 10 mm Medium | 37.8 | 7.6 | Uniform polish, no delamination |
| 2 | 10 mm Medium | 41.2 | 8.2 | Minor medial polish |
| 3 | 10 mm Medium | 39.6 | 7.9 | No unusual surface findings |
| 4 | 10 mm Medium | 43.1 | 8.6 | Light anterior contact polish |
| 5 | 10 mm Medium | 38.9 | 7.8 | No unusual surface findings |
| 6 | 10 mm Medium | 40.5 | 8.1 | Uniform polish, no delamination |

Mean corrected wear volume was 40.2 mm³ at five million cycles, with a station-to-station range of 37.8 to 43.1 mm³. Mean calculated wear rate was 8.0 mm³ per million cycles.

The control specimens showed the expected fluid uptake behavior. Meridian applied the soak-control correction before reporting the final values above. Raw mass-loss data and the control data are retained in Meridian report MTL-KF-19-044 and the accompanying electronic worksheet.

Surface Findings

Visual review did not identify cracking, pitting, delamination, or gross material loss on any test insert. The expected polished contact regions were present on the medial and lateral bearing surfaces. Station 4 had slightly more visible anterior polish than the other stations, but its gravimetric result remained within the overall range and there was no associated damage pattern.

There were no mechanical interruptions, fixture failures, or protocol deviations reported by Meridian during the five-million-cycle run.

Conclusion

The KneeFlex tibial insert demonstrated acceptable wear performance under the tested ISO 14243 simulator conditions through five million cycles. Results are consistent across all six stations and support continued use of the current insert geometry and material specification.

Meridian’s final signed report, MTL-KF-19-044, and the station-level measurement workbook have been placed in the KneeFlex design verification folder. No additional simulator testing is recommended from these results alone.

Apex Revenue Impact Model — Q4 2022 Scenarios
Prepared by: Hannah Berg, FP&A Manager
Date: October 14, 2022
To: Owen Park, CFO
Subject: Apex Revenue Impact Model - Q4 2022 Scenarios

Attached: `Apex_Revenue_Impact_Model_Q4_2022_v5.xlsx`

Owen,

Per our discussion, I refreshed the Apex model using September actuals and the current field forecast. The model is intended to frame revenue exposure through FY24; it does not attempt to estimate claim severity or timing.

Apex FY22 is now expected to close at approximately $71.0M, versus the $96.0M peak in FY20. The decline began before the June cup recall in the underlying order data. The more pronounced step-down follows the September 2021 labeling update and what Sales characterizes as increased surgeon caution after the NJR data circulated. The recall remains a separate, lot-specific assumption in the model, although several field teams report customers are not making that distinction.

Summary output ($M):

| Scenario | FY22E | FY23E | FY24E | FY22–FY24 Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Status quo / current label | 71.0 | 62.4 | 60.1 | (15%) |
| Label-driven decline | 71.0 | 54.7 | 45.9 | (35%) |
| Full market withdrawal | 71.0 | 48.3 | 42.6 | (40%) |

The status quo case assumes current labeling remains in place, no broad commercial action, and modest attrition offset by existing account utilization. It is the closest to the current Sales operating plan, though I would not characterize it as the base case with high confidence.

The label-driven decline case assumes continued loss of new implanters, lower utilization among accounts that have moved Apex to a limited-use position, and increasing price concessions where distributors seek to retain volume. This case reflects the present trajectory in the Southeast and selected Midwest accounts more closely than the operating plan.

The withdrawal case assumes no new commercial placements after an orderly market action, with only limited residual revenue from contracted inventory and replacement requirements. This is necessarily a planning construct, not a recommendation regarding product status.

For reserve adequacy testing, I recommend using the full withdrawal scenario as the conservative revenue sensitivity. It produces the lowest contribution available to absorb claims-related costs and avoids relying on a recovery in surgeon confidence that we are not seeing in the current forecast submissions.

I have kept the $18M Q3 reserve as a separate line item in the workbook and have not assumed any insurance recoveries. We can walk through the account-level assumptions Monday if helpful.

Hannah

Priya, Dana—

Forwarding the final Meridian report for P-001. See attached: MTL-16-4478_ApexHip_P-001_Final.pdf.

The result is good: 2.1 mm3/million cycles mean wear against the 5.8 reference value we provided for ClassicHip, with no runaways or visible abnormal surface damage through 5M cycles. It follows the DR-3 protocol and should support the wear-performance section of the 510(k) package as drafted.

I still think it would be worth doing a small follow-on study at higher angles, because actual cup placement varies more than the idealized setup, surgeon to surgeon and patient to patient. Could be an R&D item once we are through clearance/launch rather than holding the current package.

Tom

Human Resources — Confidential Personnel Record

Date: October 4, 2022
From: Lisa Tran, HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality
Subject: Performance Improvement Plan Closure - Complaint Handling Specialist
Employee: Denise Ortiz, Complaint Handling Specialist, Quality & Complaint Handling
Manager: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling

This memorandum documents the conclusion of Denise Ortiz’s 90-day Performance Improvement Plan (“PIP”), effective October 4, 2022.

Denise was placed on a PIP on July 5, 2022, following recurring missed MDR triage deadlines and an accumulated TrackWise intake backlog. The concern was not the quality of Denise’s clinical documentation when completed, but timeliness in completing initial complaint assessment, escalation, and routing steps under the Complaint Handling procedure. During the review preceding the PIP, Denise’s on-time triage rate was 62%, with several items requiring reassignment or manager follow-up before the applicable MDR decision window could be confirmed.

The PIP established the following expectations:

1. Complete initial triage and routing of assigned complaint records within the procedural timeframe, absent documented clinical or customer follow-up needs.
2. Maintain an on-time triage rate of at least 85% for the review period.
3. Review the open TrackWise queue with Priya Raman twice weekly and identify items requiring support before deadlines lapse.
4. Escalate potential MDR-reportable events promptly and document the rationale for any pending determination.
5. Participate in refresher training on complaint intake, MDR decision trees, and queue-management practices.

Denise completed the required refresher training on July 12, 2022. She also adopted a daily priority review and used the twice-weekly queue meetings to flag records awaiting operative notes, product identification, or clinical follow-up.

Performance during the PIP review period was as follows:

| Review Period | Assigned TrackWise Records | Triaged On Time | On-Time Rate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Pre-PIP baseline | 87 | 54 | 62% |
| July 5–August 4 | 46 | 38 | 83% |
| August 5–September 4 | 51 | 45 | 88% |
| September 5–October 3 | 47 | 43 | 91% |

Across the 90-day period, Denise closed or timely triaged 126 of 144 assigned TrackWise records. The remaining records were documented as pending external information or reassigned pursuant to the escalation process; none were permitted to lapse without manager visibility. Priya has confirmed that Denise’s recent work has been more consistent, that potential MDR matters are being surfaced earlier, and that the prior backlog associated with Denise’s queue has been substantially resolved.

Based on the foregoing, HR and management recommend that Denise’s PIP be closed successfully effective October 4, 2022. Denise is expected to sustain the performance improvements described above and continue to follow established complaint-handling and MDR triage procedures.

Priya will conduct a follow-up performance check-in with Denise in approximately 90 days, during the first week of January 2023. HR will remain available to support that discussion and will retain this memorandum and related PIP documentation in Denise’s confidential personnel file.

Lisa Tran
HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality

-----Original Message-----
From: Tom Halvorsen <thalvorsen@veridianortho.com>
Sent: Monday, January 10, 2022 9:14 AM
To: Priya Raman <praman@veridianortho.com>; Carlos Mendes <cmendes@veridianortho.com>
Subject: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

MEMORANDUM

TO: Priya Raman, Director of Quality & Complaint Handling; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
DATE: January 10, 2022
SUBJECT: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

I am writing to formally revisit the open engineering posture surrounding ECO-2019-118. It has now been nearly three years since I submitted the initial Engineering Change Order proposal in February 2019, and our Design History File (DHF) index still does not accurately capture where we stand on this.

To recap the technical history: during the development phase leading up to Design Review 3 (DR-3) in November 2016, our wear simulator protocol was established strictly under ISO 14242-1 standard parameters, testing acetabular component placement at a nominal 45° inclination angle only. The Meridian Testing Labs reports confirmed acceptable volumetric wear under those ideal, nominal conditions, which supported our 510(k) clearance (K162447). However, as I flagged in my February 2019 re-analysis memo, testing the system under steeper acetabular cup inclinations—specifically 55°—produced severe edge-loading dynamics. The wear simulator data showed a 4× to 6× increase in gravimetric and volumetric metal wear rates compared to the 45° baseline, driven by localized contact stresses at the cup rim during microseparation cycles.

ECO-2019-118 proposed an immediate modification to the acetabular rim radius and polar clearance profile to mitigate edge-loading wear at non-ideal cup angles (which clinical data shows occur frequently in real-world patient anatomy).

In mid-2019, leadership decided to formally defer ECO-2019-118. The stated rationale at the time centered on commercial friction: tooling changeout costs, scrap write-downs, and especially the timeline required for full mechanical and simulator requalification, which would have disrupted peak production volumes.

Here is my primary concern today: as of January 2022, three full years after we identified the 4–6× wear multiplier under steep angles, no design change has been implemented. None. The product currently being shipped from Warsaw and Cork retains the exact rim geometry cleared in 2017.

Furthermore, I reviewed the ApexHip DHF index in Agile last week and noticed ECO-2019-118 is marked as "Closed / Superseded by Commercial Labeling Review." This is factually incorrect and creates an audit vulnerability. The engineering risk was never resolved or designed out; it was *deferred*. We should not be relying solely on post-market technique guides or surgeon education to manage a mechanical wear condition that we know occurs once the cup tilts past 50°.

I recommend two immediate corrective actions:
1. Re-open the DHF index entry for ECO-2019-118 and formally designate its status as "Deferred — Pending Clinical Registry / Post-Market Review," explicitly noting that the original ISO 14242 protocol tested only 45° inclination and did not evaluate edge-loading conditions.
2. Reconvene the cross-functional engineering review team (Quality, Product Management, R&D) to decide whether we are going to requalify the modified rim tooling or leave the deferred status on the permanent record.

We have known about the edge-loading wear multiplier since early 2019. Leaving the change order in administrative limbo without a clear engineering resolution is a significant unaddressed risk.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
Human Resources — Confidential Manager Check-in Note

Date: August 15, 2022
Prepared by: Lisa Tran, HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality
Subject: Mid-Year Check-in - Tom Halvorsen

I met with Tom on August 11 as part of the informal mid-year check-in cycle for the ApexHip engineering group. This was not a formal performance review and no action is required in Workday at this time.

Tom continues to perform strongly in his Senior Design Engineer role. His technical knowledge of the Apex system, including historical design decisions, wear-testing methodology, and supporting DHF documentation, remains unusually deep. His manager reports that he is responsive on technical questions, thorough with data review, and dependable when cross-functional teams need historical context. Tom has also been helpful to newer engineers who are trying to understand the legacy KBT coating work and the relationship between material specifications and product performance.

The main concern coming out of the conversation is engagement and role fit. Tom stated that he is increasingly interested in moving out of the day-to-day Apex work and into a role with more forward-looking development responsibility. He specifically mentioned Advanced Materials as an area he would like to explore, particularly work involving coatings, tribology, and test-method development.

Tom did not characterize this as an immediate resignation risk, but he was candid that he has felt discouraged and “stuck” since the recall announcement. He described the current work as highly reactive and said he is spending more time revisiting prior decisions than doing engineering he considers productive. He was careful not to raise a specific complaint about any individual. His comments were more generally about the volume of follow-up requests, the pace of cross-functional review, and his concern that technical input is sometimes sought after decisions have already been framed.

I recommend that Tom’s manager schedule a focused retention conversation before the end of August. The discussion should acknowledge his contributions, clarify near-term expectations, and ask directly what type of work would make the next 12–18 months sustainable for him. Given his background, a lateral move or partial assignment to Advanced Materials could be a reasonable option by Q4, subject to business need and headcount planning.

I will connect separately with the Advanced Materials HR lead regarding anticipated openings and will keep this note confidential within the appropriate management/HR group.

From: Dr. Leon Adeyemi <ladeyemi@veridianortho.com>
To: Dana Okonkwo <dokonkwo@veridianortho.com>, Greg Novak <gnovak@veridianortho.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Aug 2021 14:22:18 -0400
Subject: Literature scan supporting registry signal ahead of September meeting

Dana, Greg,

Ahead of the Registry Signal Review next month, I pulled together a brief scan of the orthopedic literature examining edge-loading wear mechanisms and systemic cobalt/chromium ion elevation in large-diameter metal-on-metal systems.

There are clear published parallels to what Greg is tracking in the NJR dataset and the steep wear gradient Tom Halvorsen documented in his 2019 simulator re-analysis at elevated cup abduction angles (>50°). In particular, the clinical community has documented that when steep acetabular inclination induces stripe wear and micro-separation, local tissue necrosis and pseudotumor formation correlate heavily with serum Co and Cr spikes, even before frank mechanical loosening shows up on radiographs.

I strongly recommend our presentation packet explicitly reference at least two foundational papers—likely Hart et al. (JBJS 2012) on edge loading and ion thresholds, and Langton et al. (BJJ 2011) regarding component positioning and bearing diameter.

Regardless of whether the committee leans toward continuing commercial distribution under an updated surgical technique and tighter labeling guidance (e.g., rigid cup positioning safe zones to mitigate steep inclination) or favors a more conservative action, our clinical rationale must be defensible against the external peer-reviewed consensus. We cannot appear to evaluate the registry revision curve in an epidemiological vacuum.

I will distill these citations into a one-page summary table for Greg to include with the pre-read materials.

Best regards,

Leon

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
CHANGE CONTROL BOARD — MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: ECO-2019-118 Review (ApexHip Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry)
Date: April 2, 2019
Time: 10:00–11:15 AM
Location: Warsaw HQ, Building 2, Engineering Conference Room
Recorded by: Tom Halvorsen

Attendees: Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer), Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling), Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip), Devon Mitchell (Sr. Regulatory Specialist), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs)

1. Background
Halvorsen presented the February 2019 wear-test re-analysis showing 4–6x increased wear rates at 55-degree cup inclination compared to the 45-degree standard used in the original ISO 14242 protocol (DR-3, Nov 2016). ECO-2019-118 was opened to evaluate a proposed rim geometry modification intended to reduce edge-loading wear at higher inclination angles.

2. Discussion
Halvorsen summarized the Meridian Labs data supporting the wear increase and noted the change would require re-tooling of the cup mold and a new round of bench testing, estimated at 4–6 months and roughly $650K in NRE. Mitchell raised the question of whether the change would trigger a new 510(k) versus a letter-to-file determination; Okonkwo stated that a geometry change of this nature would likely require a new submission given potential impact on predicate equivalence, adding regulatory timeline risk.

Raman reported that current TrackWise complaint volume for metal-ion-related issues remained low (single-digit cluster from the 2018 Atlanta group, TW-2018-0912 et seq.) and that no clear registry signal had yet emerged domestically. Mendes noted commercial concerns about disrupting the "Active Life" launch momentum and asked whether the wear data reflected real-world inclination angles or worst-case bench conditions only. Halvorsen acknowledged the bench testing used a fixed 55-degree angle chosen to stress-test edge loading and that clinical inclination distribution data was not yet available.

The group discussed cost, regulatory burden, and the absence of a confirmed clinical signal at this time as factors weighing against an immediate design change.

3. Resolution
The Change Control Board voted to DEFER ECO-2019-118. The board found insufficient clinical signal and complaint trend evidence at this time to justify the cost and regulatory risk of the proposed rim geometry change. The board will revisit the decision upon receipt of additional wear data and updated complaint trending.

Vote: 4 in favor of deferral (Raman, Mendes, Mitchell, Okonkwo), 1 opposed (Halvorsen), recommending continued monitoring.

4. Action Items
- Raman to compile a quarterly complaint trend summary for ApexHip metal-ion/wear-related events, due end of Q2 2019.
- Halvorsen to continue informal wear testing at varied inclination angles outside formal ECO scope, results to be shared at next review.
- Mitchell to note deferral rationale in the DHF change log for ECO-2019-118.
- Next review to be scheduled upon receipt of updated data, no later than Q4 2019.

Minutes approved by consensus of attendees present.
